memory_candidates.content: When a task's edit target is the agent-system SOURCE STORE (resolved via .claude-extensions.json's source_dir, e.g. /home/benjamin/.config/nvim containing agent-system/), that store is a SEPARATE git repository from the deploy-target repo running the dispatch. git-commit-phase.sh / git-commit-scoped.sh only stage within the deploy-target repo's own working tree, so a source-store file is always reported as an unmatched/dropped pathspec there -- this is expected, not an error. Each phase needs TWO commits: one in the deploy-target repo (via git-commit-phase.sh, covering only the task-dir plan/progress/handoff files) and a separate one made directly in the source-store repo with an explicit, narrowly-scoped `git add -- <files>` + `git commit` (never -A), using the same `task {N} phase {P}: {name}` message convention.

guard-destructive-git.sh's git-commit -a/-am detector (regex (^|[^-])-[a-zA-Z]*a[a-zA-Z]*([[:space:]]|$)) false-positives on ordinary hyphenated prose in a commit message BODY, not just on an actual -a/-am flag -- e.g. 'deploy-target repository' or 'Batch-aware deferral' trip it even though the command has no such flag. Workaround: avoid hyphens immediately followed by a word containing 'a' and then whitespace/end-of-line in commit message text (rewrite 'deploy-target' as 'deploy target', etc.), or write the message to a file and use `git commit -F <file>` after confirming with `grep -noE -- '(^|[^-])-[a-zA-Z]*a[a-zA-Z]*([[:space:]]|$)' <file>` that it returns no match.

When a plan's Scope Hypothesis asserts a shared helper function (e.g. a logging/warning function) has exactly one caller, re-verify with a fresh grep before applying a caller-specific behavior change directly inside the shared function -- a second caller can rely on the function's CURRENT behavior for a reason the plan's author never saw (e.g. an existing test asserting a specific output channel for batch-attributability). When a second caller is found and its needs genuinely differ, the safer fix is a new, separately-named sibling function used only by the caller that needs the new behavior, leaving the original function and its other callers completely untouched, rather than parameterizing the shared function's severity/behavior.
